newsitem.title: INDIA: India opposition backtracks on no-trust vote move.
newsitem.headline: India opposition backtracks on no-trust vote move.

text.p: India's main opposition party on Thursday backtracked on a bid to topple Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda, saying it would not press for a no-confidence vote against the government it had planned for Friday.

"We are not interested in a no-confidence motion early in the budget session," former prime minister Atal Behari Vajpayee, the leader of the biggest opposition group, the Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), told Reuters. "We want it as the last weapon."

Speaking after an address by President Shankar Dayal Sharma at the start of parliament's budget session on Thursday, Vajpayee said the BJP had pursuaded a socialist ally to drop the no-trust move for the moment.
Finance Minister P. Chidambaram is due to present the budget for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March) on February 28.
Asked if he expected Deve Gowda's 13-member alliance government to fall during the three-month long budget session, Vajpayee said: "It will survive for a while."

Parliament's lower house Speaker Purno Sangma had told reporters earlier on Thursday that he intended to take up the no-confidence motion by Samta Party leader George Fernandes for discussion on Friday.
But Samta party officials said they expected Fernandes to withdraw the move.
Deve Gowda's minority United Front alliance controls some 178 deputies in the 545-member Lok Sabha, or lower house. It is reluctantly supported by the Congress party which has 142 votes.
The BJP with its allies has 194 votes.
Congress spokesman Vithal Gadgil told Reuters on Wednesday that he expected the government to survive the budget session which is expected to end on May 12.

Gadgil's remarks were the strongest indication so far that the Congress, which suffered its worst-ever defeat in last year's general elections, was not about to precipitate the mid-term election that would follow if Deve Gowda were to lose his majority.

India's oldest political machine, Congress is reeling from a string of financial scandals dogging its leading politicians, and suffered a humiliating defeat earlier this month in the northern farming state of Punjab.
Congress's pledge to keep Deve Gowda's government going seemed to have little effect on the BJP.

"The shadow of uncertainty is looming large on this government's chances of survival," said Krishan Lal Sharma, vice president of the BJP, which is the largest single group in parliament's lower house.

Sharma said the BJP would back the no-confidence motion in the hope of widening a rift between the Congress and the United Front over a host of economic issues and a 1986 artillery deal known as the "Bofors scandal".

The federal investigating agency this month revealed the names of five people who it said had received payments from Sweden's Bofors AB in the $1.3 billion howitzer deal. It said more names could be revealed later.
Bofors said last week it saw no need to reopen the investigation into the contract, and added that the firm had paid money as final payments to its agents, not as bribes.
Congress politicians say the scandal has been deliberately revived by Deve Gowda to embarrass their party. Congress lost the 1989 general elections largely over the Bofors issue.
